claims.text: MoS2 or WS2 are high-temperature-stable solid lubricants.
Incorporating MoS2 or WS2 into a high-strength ceramic matrix by spark plasma sintering will produce a self-lubricating composite.
The resulting composite will retain high mechanical strength.
The resulting composite will significantly reduce friction and wear from room temperature to above 800 °C.
The initial ceramic matrix has excellent mechanical properties.
The initial ceramic matrix has limited self-lubricating capability at elevated temperatures.
Spark plasma sintering can yield a fine and homogeneous dispersion of MoS2 or WS2 within the ceramic matrix.
A fine, homogeneous lubricant-phase dispersion facilitates self-lubrication while preserving the ceramic matrix's structural integrity.
Under high-temperature sliding, dispersed MoS2 or WS2 particles form lubricating films at contact interfaces.
The interfacial lubricating films reduce friction and wear.
The ceramic matrix maintains high mechanical strength during high-temperature sliding.
Combining lubricant-film formation with matrix strength overcomes the trade-off between mechanical strength and lubrication efficiency.
Compared with the pure ceramic matrix, the composite will have lower friction coefficients across the tested temperature range.
Compared with the pure ceramic matrix, the composite will have lower wear rates across the tested temperature range.
The composite will suffer only a minor reduction in mechanical strength relative to the pure ceramic matrix.
Lubricant effectiveness may diminish beyond the tested temperature range or under extreme cyclic thermal stresses.
Successful performance depends critically on obtaining a uniform dispersion of the lubricant phases.
